captions.instagram:
What is friction?

Friction is the force that holds before it slips. Pull a block with a spring scale and watch the grip peak then drop, stop a car on dry roads and ice, float a crankshaft on oil, hold a boat with one hand and three turns of rope, and bust the myth that pressure makes ice slippery.

→ Pull a block: friction grows to match you, up to μs × N. Then it slips, and friction drops.
→ Tilt the ramp. The block lets go exactly when tan θ reaches μs, whatever it weighs.
→ Braking distance is v² ÷ 2μg: on ice, a car at 60 km/h needs eight times as far to stop.
→ Too fast on worn tyres, a wedge of water lifts the tyre off the road: aquaplaning.
→ Brake again and again with no time to cool, and friction heats the discs until they glow.

Play with it yourself. It's free and open source: glassbox.how/frictionclear (link in bio)

youtubeLong.title: What is friction? (interactive explainer)
youtubeLong.description:
Friction is the force that holds before it slips. Pull a block with a spring scale and watch the grip peak then drop, stop a car on dry roads and ice, float a crankshaft on oil, hold a boat with one hand and three turns of rope, and bust the myth that pressure makes ice slippery.

▶ Play with the interactive version: https://glassbox.how/e/frictionclear/
⌘ Source code (MIT): https://github.com/bdeeps/frictionclear

In this video:
• Grip, then slip. Friction resists sliding.
• Grip on the road. Tyres drive, steer and stop through static friction: μ about 0.8 dry, 0.5 wet, 0.1 on ice.
• Friction we fight. Rolling needs about 1% of the weight for a car, a hundredth of dragging it.
• Friction we need. Each step pushes the ground back so the ground pushes you forward, needing μ ≈ 0.18.
• Myths and limits. Friction doesn't depend on contact area.
